question: A 15-year-old teenager presents for a sports physical. His blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg, temperature is 36.5°C (97.7°F), and heart rate is 100/min. On cardiac auscultation, an early diastolic heart sound is heard over the cardiac apex while the patient is in the left lateral decubitus position. A transthoracic echocardiogram is performed which shows an ejection fraction of 60% without any other abnormalities. Which of the following is the end-systolic volume in this patient if his cardiac output is 6 L/min?

enhanced_information: Using the cardiac output of 6 L/min and a heart rate of 100 beats/min, the stroke volume is calculated as 60 mL/beat. With an ejection fraction of 60%, the end-diastolic volume is calculated as 100 mL. Therefore, the end-systolic volume, calculated as the difference between end-diastolic volume and stroke volume, is 40 mL.
analysis: To determine the end-systolic volume (ESV) in this patient, we start by calculating the stroke volume (SV) using the provided cardiac output (CO) and heart rate (HR). The formula for stroke volume is SV = CO / HR. Given a CO of 6 L/min and an HR of 100 beats/min, the SV is 60 mL/beat. The ejection fraction (EF), which is the proportion of blood pumped out of the ventricle with each heartbeat, is given as 60%. The formula for end-diastolic volume (EDV) using EF is EDV = SV / EF. Substituting the known values, EDV = 60 mL / 0.6 = 100 mL. The ESV can then be calculated using the formula ESV = EDV - SV. Substituting the known values, ESV = 100 mL - 60 mL = 40 mL. This calculation aligns with standard medical formulas and principles used in cardiology for assessing cardiac function, and the enhanced information provided confirms the correctness of this approach.
